Team-authored code lives entirely in C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/FTC_2026_2027/TeamCode/src/main/java/org/firstinspires/ftc/teamcode/ — 45 files, ~14,000 lines. The one large file that is NOT team-authored is pedroPathing/Tuning.java (1792 lines, @author Baron Henderson, vendored Pedro tuning menu).
summary: This repo is the opposite of thin: outside the stock SDK it is ~14k lines of dense, hand-written, heavily-Javadoc'd FTC code with a real architecture — a `Superstructure` mode state machine, one class per mechanism, a single 1156-line `RobotConstants`, a Limelight vision layer, Pedro Pathing autos with AprilTag pose correction, and five interchangeable shooter templates. Critically, the README and nearly every util class say outright that these abstractions were **ported FROM the author's FRC template** (`0000-XXXX-Robot-Template`): `AllianceFlipUtil`, `InterpolatingTable`, `AimingCalculator`, `RobotState`, `Superstructure`, `Sensors` all carry an explicit "Ported from the FRC template's X.java" section. So for a new FRC library, most of what's here is a *round trip*, not new material. What IS genuinely new and worth pulling back into FRC is the hardware-resilience layer (`SafeHardware` + `isAvailable()` on every mechanism + an init-time health report), the explicit once-per-loop input caching discipline (`BulkReads` + cached interlock samples in `Superstructure.update()`), the dead-man manual-control pattern in `Climber`, the single-chokepoint soft-limit helper repeated in `Turret`/`Climber`/`Elevator`, and an unusually valuable corpus of ~15 in-code post-mortems marked `*** BUG THAT WAS FIXED HERE ***` that read as a spec for footguns a library should make structurally impossible. The cost side is equally clear: the same ~120 lines of null-guard/ticks-conversion/soft-limit/homing/stall boilerplate is retyped in six mechanisms, the five shooters duplicate an identical spin-up→feed→retract state machine and an identical hardcoded RPM table, and every tuning value is a Java constant requiring a rebuild-and-redeploy.
stack: FTC SDK 11.1.0 (`org.firstinspires.ftc:RobotCore/Hardware/Vision/FtcCommon:11.1.0`), Pedro Pathing `com.pedropathing:ftc:2.1.2` + `com.pedropathing:telemetry:1.0.0`, Panels `com.bylazar:fullpanels:1.0.12` (custom maven `https://mymaven.bylazar.com/releases`). Java 8 only — `build.common.gradle` pins `sourceCompatibility/targetCompatibility JavaVersion.VERSION_1_8`, and `AimingCalculator.ShotSolution` comments "Newer Java has `record` for exactly this, but FTC still compiles against Java 8, so we write it out." AGP 8.7.0, compileSdk 34, minSdk 24, targetSdk 28. Hardware: REV Control Hub (built-in IMU via `RevHubOrientationOnRobot`), goBILDA 5203 Yellow Jacket motors (537.7 ticks/rev) + bare REV HD Hex (28 ticks/rev) for flywheels, `DcMotorEx` everywhere current/velocity is needed, plain `Servo` for feeders/hood/pivot/Blinkin, `DistanceSensor`/`TouchSensor`/`LED`, Limelight 3A configured as an Ethernet Device. No vendordeps/*.json (FTC uses plain Gradle deps), no .vscode, no CLAUDE.md, no swerve config, no PathPlanner, no tuner-project.json, no unit tests, no simulation.
constraints: Java 8 source level is hard-pinned in build.common.gradle — no records, no var, no switch expressions, no sealed types. Any shared library that must also compile for FTC has to be Java 8-clean; an FRC-only library (Java 17) can use records, but the FTC port would then need a parallel hand-written version, exactly as AimingCalculator.ShotSolution shows.

Hardware is discovered by string name at runtime, not constructed by ID — `SafeHardware.tryGet(hardwareMap, DcMotorEx.class, name)` with `name == null` meaning 'this robot does not have this part'. Any config abstraction must support 'device is legitimately absent' as a first-class state, not an error.

Two-step encoder reset is mandatory and easy to get wrong: `setMode(STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER)` then immediately `setMode(RUN_USING_ENCODER)`, or the motor silently refuses power. Called out in readme.md and repeated verbatim in Elevator.init, Turret.init, Climber.init.

Nothing may block: `readme.md` states 'Never use sleep() inside loop()'. Every multi-step action must be a call-me-every-loop state machine (Elevator.updateHoming, SingleShooter.update, Indexer.update, VisionCorrectedAuto.autonomousPathUpdate).

Loop budget is ~20 ms and every encoder/I2C read is a 1-3 ms bus round trip. BulkReads.java documents that the competition TeleOp does 10+ encoder reads per loop; the fix (MANUAL bulk caching) is fragile — 'forgetting to call clearCache freezes every sensor reading forever'.

Units are inches / degrees / seconds / RPM throughout FTC, versus meters / radians in the FRC template — AimingCalculator says so explicitly ('The FRC version uses metres and radians, matching WPILib'). Any shared math library needs an explicit unit boundary rather than bare doubles.

Three mutually incompatible field coordinate frames coexist: Limelight/FIRST (origin at field center, ±72 in), Pedro Pathing (origin at a corner, 0-144 in, rotated a quarter turn), and raw IMU yaw (zeroed wherever the robot faced at INIT). RobotConstants.VisionConstants documents the conversion as `pedroX = ftcY + 72; pedroY = -ftcX + 72` plus a 90-degree yaw offset.

Game-specific values must be isolatable and unknown until kickoff — every unknown is tagged `[KICKOFF]` inside RobotConstants.VisionConstants (tag IDs, goal heights, ball color, mirror axis) so the logic never needs editing.

The project must run on a half-built robot: readme.md promises 'a chassis with nothing but four drive motors runs every OpMode in the project', and every Test OpMode is expected to work with only its one mechanism configured.
No simulation exists and none is possible on the FTC side — all validation is on physical hardware, which is why the Test OpModes and the `[MEASURE THIS]` markers carry so much weight.

patterns.name: SafeHardware — non-throwing hardware lookup + global missing-device registry + init health report
patterns.whatItDoes: Generic `tryGet` wraps `hardwareMap.get()` in try/catch and returns null instead of throwing; a null name is treated as 'not fitted' and deliberately NOT recorded as missing. A static list accumulates every device that failed, and `reportHealth(telemetry)` prints a degraded-mode banner at init. Every mechanism then exposes `isAvailable()` and makes every public method a safe no-op when false.
patterns.whereSeen: C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/FTC_2026_2027/TeamCode/src/main/java/org/firstinspires/ftc/teamcode/util/SafeHardware.java (all 140 lines); used in MecanumDrive.init, Elevator.init, Turret.init, Climber.init, Indexer.init, Intake.init, Flywheel.init, Hood.init, StatusLEDs.init, LimelightVision.init; reported in BioBuzzCompetition.init line 92
patterns.libraryValue: This is the single most transferable idea in the repo and it has no WPILib equivalent. FRC's failure mode is different in shape (CAN devices construct fine and then silently return stale/zero data) but identical in consequence, and teams handle it worse: a disconnected Falcon usually produces a mechanism that quietly does nothing. A library could own the whole thing — a `Devices` registry that records construction/connection failures, a `HealthReport` published to NT/Elastic at robotInit, and a `Mechanism` base class whose `isAvailable()` gates commands. The subtle detail worth copying exactly: the interlock consumers must treat 'absent' as 'satisfied', not 'waiting' — `Turret.isAtTarget()` returns TRUE when there is no turret specifically so the shoot interlock does not stall forever on a mechanism the robot does not have.

patterns.name: Superstructure — enum mode machine that commands EVERY actuator on EVERY branch
patterns.whatItDoes: A single `RobotMode` enum (IDLE/INTAKING/EJECTING/AIMING/SHOOTING/SCORING/CLIMB_READY/CLIMBING/MANUAL) owns all nine mechanisms. `update(heading)` does a fixed four-phase cycle: refresh hardware-reading subsystems, sample interlock inputs once, run automatic transitions, then `applyMode()` drives every mechanism. Setting the mode is the entire external interface; TeleOp sets it from buttons and autonomous from its path state machine.
patterns.whereSeen: C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/FTC_2026_2027/TeamCode/src/main/java/org/firstinspires/ftc/teamcode/Superstructure.java lines 156-317; consumed by robots/biobuzz/BioBuzzCompetition.java
patterns.libraryValue: The interesting content is not the state machine, it is the invariant discovered by breaking it. Three separate documented bugs are all the same defect: a mode that failed to command an actuator left that actuator LATCHED at whatever the previous mode set. `INTAKING`/`EJECTING`/`SCORING`/`CLIMBING` didn't command the turret, so switching out of `AIMING` mid-track left it turning into its travel limit; `MANUAL` didn't stop the intake/indexer/flywheel, so 'all automation off' actually meant 'automation frozen mid-action'. WPILib command-based only partially prevents this via default commands and requirements, and teams that write a superstructure state machine on top of it lose that protection entirely. A library could enforce completeness structurally: a mode returns a map of subsystem→setpoint and the framework applies a declared safe default to every subsystem the map omits, so 'forgot to command it' becomes impossible rather than a comment.

patterns.name: Once-per-loop input cache, applied at three levels
patterns.whatItDoes: Three layered caching disciplines, each added after a measured loop-time problem. (1) `BulkReads` puts every LynxModule in MANUAL bulk-caching mode and requires `clearCache(hubs)` as the literal first line of `loop()`. (2) `Indexer.update()` reads both distance sensors and motor current into `cachedEntryMm/cachedExitMm/cachedCurrentAmps` and every getter serves from the cache. (3) `Superstructure.update()` samples `shooter.isReadyToShoot()` and `turret.isAtTarget()` into per-loop fields so the interlock, the LEDs, and telemetry all read the same values.
patterns.whereSeen: util/BulkReads.java; mechanisms/indexer/Indexer.java lines 100-106 and 162-179; Superstructure.java lines 101-104, 166-172, 356-359; entry point at robots/biobuzz/BioBuzzCompetition.java lines 84 and 109
patterns.libraryValue: This is AdvantageKit's IO-inputs pattern independently rediscovered from first principles, and the comments give the two reasons that matter: cost ('one loop of a test OpMode performed five I2C reads — a quarter of the whole 20 ms loop budget') AND consistency ('the interlock, LEDs and telemetry all agree'). An FRC library should make the consistency argument first-class, not just the performance one: a `Superstructure` that asks `isReadyToShoot()` three times in a loop can get three different answers across a signal refresh boundary, and the resulting bug looks like a flaky shooter. Codifying 'sample once at the top of the cycle into an immutable snapshot, then decide' — even for teams not using AdvantageKit — is worth a small `@AutoInputs`-style helper.

patterns.name: Dead-man manual control: store the request, apply-and-clear inside update()
patterns.whatItDoes: `Climber.manualControl(power)` does not touch the motor — it only stores `manualPower` and sets mode MANUAL. `update()` is the sole place power reaches the motor: it applies `limitAtTravelEnds(manualPower, getHeightInches())` then zeroes `manualPower`. If the OpMode stops calling `manualControl()`, output decays to zero within one ~20 ms loop.
patterns.whereSeen: C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/FTC_2026_2027/TeamCode/src/main/java/org/firstinspires/ftc/teamcode/mechanisms/climber/Climber.java lines 174-215 and 300-312
patterns.libraryValue: The bug comment explains why this matters and it applies verbatim to FRC: `setPower`/`set()` LATCHES, so a manual-control method that writes the motor directly keeps winching at the last commanded power forever if the caller stops calling — and the soft limits were only checked at the moment the stick moved, not at the position reached since. WPILib partly mitigates this with the motor safety watchdog and default commands, but hand-rolled manual overrides on climbers and elevators (which every team writes) reintroduce it. A library primitive — `DeadManOutput` / `TimedLatch` that decays to a safe value after N ms without a fresh write, with the limit check re-evaluated at apply time rather than command time — is small, generic, and prevents a genuinely dangerous failure.

patterns.name: Single-chokepoint soft limit that allows escape toward the middle
patterns.whatItDoes: One private method per mechanism zeroes power that would push past a travel end, while still allowing motion back toward center. Every control path in the class — vision tracking, closed-loop angle hold, and manual — routes through it, so a newly added control mode cannot skip the check.
patterns.whereSeen: mechanisms/turret/Turret.java `limitPowerAtTravelEnds` lines 276-284 (used by applyTrackingPower, goToAngle, manualControl); mechanisms/climber/Climber.java `limitAtTravelEnds` lines 254-262 (used by driveToward and the MANUAL case); mechanisms/elevator/Elevator.java lines 148-171 inlines the same logic plus a limit-switch override
patterns.libraryValue: Two design details deserve to be library defaults rather than rediscovered per team: (a) an asymmetric limit — never block the direction that recovers — because symmetric clamping traps a mechanism at its limit with no way out, and (b) a single choke point so limits are structurally unskippable. Elevator additionally shows the right precedence: a physical limit switch overrides the encoder ('encoders can drift; a switch is ground truth') and re-zeros — but only when drift exceeds 0.25 in, because the naive version re-ran `STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER` (two bus writes) every loop the operator held the stick down. That's exactly the kind of detail a shared `SoftLimitedMechanism`/`LimitSwitchHoming` abstraction should bake in.

patterns.name: InterpolatingTable + distance-keyed lookup for RPM, hood angle and flight time
patterns.whatItDoes: A `TreeMap<Double,Double>` with `floorEntry`/`ceilingEntry` lerp, deliberately CLAMPING at the ends rather than extrapolating ('extrapolating past your data means guessing, and a wrong guess here means a flywheel command far outside anything you have tested'), returning 0.0 on an empty table, and exposing `isEmpty()`/`size()` so consumers can detect the silent-failure case.
patterns.whereSeen: util/InterpolatingTable.java (152 lines); consumed by mechanisms/shooter/Flywheel.java (`rpmForDistance`, `loadDefaultRpmTable`), mechanisms/shooter/Hood.java (`angleForDistance`, `loadDefaultAngleTable`), and util/AimingCalculator.java (three tables injected via constructor)
patterns.libraryValue: The class itself is a reimplementation of WPILib's `InterpolatingDoubleTreeMap` (the Javadoc says so), so FRC gains nothing from the data structure. What FRC's version LACKS and this one has are the safety affordances: clamp-not-extrapolate as an explicit documented policy, `isEmpty()` surfaced so an unpopulated table is a detectable fault rather than 'shooter commands 0 RPM and the ball drops on the floor', and `addDataPoint()` designed for live capture from a test routine. A library wrapper — `ShotTable` with validity, provenance, and a live-capture hook feeding a persisted file — is a real improvement over the raw WPILib map.

patterns.name: Vision pose correction with rate limit, outlier gate, blend, and consistent-rejection recovery
patterns.whatItDoes: Wraps a Pedro `Follower`. Rate-limits corrections (0.5 s), rejects poses disagreeing with odometry by more than 24 in, otherwise blends 20% toward vision leaving heading untouched. The novel part: it counts consecutive REJECTIONS that agree with each other within 6 in — three in a row means odometry is the thing that jumped (collision, wheel slip), so it snaps fully to vision instead of locking vision out forever. The vision layer upstream independently gates on tag count (>=2), average tag distance (<=120 in), `isValid()`, and staleness (<=250 ms).
patterns.whereSeen: vision/VisionPoseCorrector.java lines 155-273; quality gates in vision/LimelightVision.java lines 140-177 (update) and 473-498 (getRobotPoseInches); constants in RobotConstants.VisionConstants lines 718-806; driven from pedroPathing/VisionCorrectedAuto.java
patterns.libraryValue: WPILib's `SwerveDrivePoseEstimator` covers blending via std-devs, but almost every FRC team writes the outlier gate by hand and virtually all of them write the version with the bug documented here: reject-forever, which disables vision at exactly the moment a collision made it most necessary. The consistent-rejection escape hatch is a genuinely good idea and is not in WPILib. Equally worth lifting are the diagnostics the class exposes for the drive team — `getCorrectionsApplied()`, `getCorrectionsRejected()`, `getLastCorrectionInches()` — with the comment 'If this stays at 0 through a whole autonomous, vision correction is not actually doing anything and you are running on odometry without realizing it.' A library `VisionGate` that publishes accept/reject counters and reject reasons would catch a very common silent failure.

patterns.name: Derived-constant discipline: declare physical facts, compute conversions
patterns.whatItDoes: Gearing constants are never typed as a final number. Ticks-per-motor-rev, gear ratio and spool/drum diameter are declared separately and the conversion is computed in the constants class itself.
patterns.whereSeen: RobotConstants.java: ElevatorConstants lines 206-222 (TICKS_PER_INCH), ClimberConstants lines 478-488, TurretConstants lines 835-846 (TICKS_PER_DEGREE), ShooterConstants lines 973-984 (DRUM_TICKS_PER_REV, DRUM_TICKS_PER_SLOT)
patterns.libraryValue: The rationale ('swap to a different spool, change one number above, everything else stays correct — typing the final number in yourself is how unit bugs get created') is exactly the argument for a typed gearing/mechanism-config object in an FRC library: `LinearMechanismConfig(motorTicksPerRev, gearRatio, drumDiameter)` producing `Distance <-> Rotations` converters, and `RotaryMechanismConfig` doing the same for the turret. Combined with a units type this eliminates a whole bug class. Note the FTC code stops one step short: the conversion is centralized but the *result* is still a bare double, so `Elevator.inchesToTicks` and `Turret` divide-by-TICKS_PER_DEGREE are still hand-written per mechanism.

patterns.name: In-code post-mortem convention: `*** BUG THAT WAS FIXED HERE ***`
patterns.whatItDoes: Roughly fifteen fixed defects are documented in place with the symptom, why it survived testing, and the generalizable lesson. Git history confirms them: commit cc56e22 'Fix 35 defects found by multi-agent adversarial code review'.
patterns.whereSeen: MecanumDrive.java lines 184-190 (mixing signs) and 305-318 (field-centric rotation); AutoAlign.java lines 141-147 (strafe projected onto LEFT while drive() is RIGHT-positive); AimingCalculator.java lines 188-195 (turret CCW vs CW); Indexer.java lines 211-221 (time-window counted one ball 3x) and 337-343 (re-entrant unjam reversed forever) and 461-467; Superstructure.java lines 108-114, 220-225, 301-308, 393-399; VisionPoseCorrector.java lines 180-188 and 255-269 (Pedro/FTC frame rotation); pedroPathing/Constants.java lines 37-56 (Follower built with null drivetrain and localizer — compiled fine, crashed every auto); VisionCorrectedAuto.java lines 109-114 and 122-133; BioBuzzCompetition.java lines 214-224 and 237-243
patterns.libraryValue: Treat this list as the requirements document for the library rather than as a pattern to copy. Five of the fifteen are sign/frame convention errors at a module boundary (CW vs CCW turret, strafe left vs right, field-centric rotation direction, Pedro vs FTC axes, IMU yaw vs field yaw) — every one of which a typed `Rotation2d`/`ChassisSpeeds`-style API or an explicit `FieldFrame`/`RobotFrame` marker type makes unrepresentable. Three are latched-actuator bugs. Two are edge-detection/debounce bugs (a time window instead of a consumed flag). Two are lifecycle/ordering bugs (`SafeHardware.resetMissingDevices()` called inside a participant erased the drivetrain's registrations; the Limelight not started before `init_loop` read it). One — `pedroPathing/Constants.java` — is a builder that compiled cleanly with two required stages omitted, producing null internals and crashing all four autos, which is a direct argument for required-stage typed builders over fluent optional setters.

painPoints.problem: The same ~120-line mechanism skeleton is retyped in six classes: null-guard every public method, ticks<->units conversion pair, min/max soft limit with escape, homing start/update pair against an optional switch, encoder-reset two-step, and stall detection.
painPoints.evidence: Elevator.java (422 lines), Turret.java (398), Climber.java (432), Indexer.java (596), Flywheel.java (274) and DrumShooter.java (500) each independently implement `isAvailable()`, private ticks conversion, a private travel-limit helper, and `resetEncoder()` with the STOP_AND_RESET/RUN_USING two-step. `Elevator.isStalled()` hardcodes its own thresholds inline — `return currentAmps > 5.0 && velocityTicksPerSecond < 10.0;` (Elevator.java:384) — while Indexer uses `IndexerConstants.STALL_CURRENT_AMPS = 6.0` and DualTowerShooter uses `TOWER_STALL_CURRENT_AMPS = 6.0`. Three stall detectors, three thresholds, one of them a magic number outside the constants file.
painPoints.libraryFix: A `PositionMechanism` base (or composable `Mechanism` + `SoftLimits` + `Homing` + `StallDetector` pieces) that takes a gearing config and a limit-switch supplier and provides units-in/units-out, asymmetric soft limits, a non-blocking homing routine, and one stall detector with a single configured threshold. Elevator/Turret/Climber then become ~60 lines of policy each instead of 400 lines of restated plumbing.

painPoints.problem: Five shooter templates duplicate an identical spin-up→feed→retract state machine and an identical hardcoded RPM table, so a fix or a re-tune has to be applied five times.
painPoints.evidence: `loadDefaultRpmTable()` with the exact same five pairs (24→2400, 48→2900, 72→3400, 96→3900, 120→4400) appears in Flywheel.java:141-145 and again in ParallelShooter.java (~line 150), and the other shooters repeat the shape. SingleShooter (280 lines), ParallelShooter (487), DrumShooter (500), RollerShooter (426) and DualTowerShooter (606) each carry their own `ShotState` enum, `ElapsedTime stateTimer`, `shotsFired` counter, and a switch whose FEEDING/RETRACTING branches are structurally identical. SingleShooter composes `Flywheel` but ParallelShooter does not — it manages two motors itself.
painPoints.libraryFix: Factor the timed-sequence part out entirely: a small `TimedSequence`/`Action` primitive (steps with a guard and a duration, advanced by `update()`) plus a reusable `VelocityMechanism` for each wheel. A shooter then declares its steps rather than re-implementing a switch. The RPM table belongs in one shared, externally-loaded `ShotTable` — right now re-tuning the shooter means editing Java in whichever of five files is in use and redeploying.

painPoints.problem: Every tunable number is a compile-time Java constant. Re-tuning at a competition means edit, rebuild, redeploy — the very scenario RobotConstants' own Javadoc says it exists to make fast.
painPoints.evidence: RobotConstants.java is 1156 lines of `public static final`, including all the values readme.md's calibration table says must be measured on the real robot (elevator ticks/inch, preset heights, turret gear ratio, camera height and pitch, indexer detect threshold, drum gear ratio, climber limits). The two lookup tables are hardcoded in Java (`Flywheel.loadDefaultRpmTable`, `Hood.loadDefaultAngleTable`). Panels' `@Configurable` — which would give live tuning — is applied only to the four Pedro autos (PedroPathingAuto_Forward/Strafe/Square, VisionCorrectedAuto) and never to any mechanism or to RobotConstants. The Test OpModes work around this with dpad increment/decrement into a local field (`ShooterTest.java:87-99` adjusts `targetRpm` by 100/25) and then instruct the student to 'Put all your pairs into Flywheel.loadDefaultRpmTable()' — i.e. transcribe by hand and rebuild.
painPoints.libraryFix: A `TunableNumber` that reads a constant by default but overrides from dashboard/NT (or a file) when a tuning-mode flag is set, plus a persisted table format so a shooter table captured live survives a redeploy without a source edit. This is the highest-leverage missing abstraction: the workflow it would replace — dpad-tune, write numbers on paper, retype into Java, rebuild — is the single biggest documented time cost in the repo.

painPoints.problem: A mode/state that forgets to command an actuator leaves it latched at the previous mode's output — three separate shipped bugs, all with the same root cause, all fixed by comment and vigilance rather than structure.
painPoints.evidence: Superstructure.java:220-225 — INTAKING (and EJECTING/SCORING/CLIMBING) never commanded the turret, so leaving AIMING mid-track left it turning into its travel limit. Superstructure.java:301-308 — MANUAL commanded only the three stick-driven mechanisms, so entering MANUAL from SHOOTING left the flywheel at speed and the indexer feeding: 'all automation off was actually automation frozen mid-action, which is worse.' Climber.java:193-207 — the MANUAL case was empty because power had been set elsewhere, so a released stick latched the winch at its last power. The current defence is a repeated hand-written comment: `turret.stop();   // see INTAKING - never leave the turret uncommanded`.
painPoints.libraryFix: Make omission impossible instead of commented. Have a mode produce a declarative setpoint map and let the framework apply a per-subsystem safe default to anything omitted; or give each subsystem a watchdog that reverts to a neutral output if it receives no command in a cycle (the `Climber` dead-man pattern, generalized). Either way the library, not the author's memory, enforces 'every mode commands every actuator.'

painPoints.problem: Sign and coordinate-frame conventions are carried in comments and bare doubles, and five separate shipped bugs came from crossing a frame boundary.
painPoints.evidence: MecanumDrive.java:184-190 (mixing formula had strafe and rotate negated), MecanumDrive.java:305-318 (field-centric rotation written for a left-positive lateral axis while `drive()` is right-positive — 'Worked perfectly at heading 0, which is exactly why it survived bench testing'), AutoAlign.java:141-147 (strafe error projected onto the LEFT unit vector, pushing the robot away from the target), AimingCalculator.java:188-196 (solver was CCW-positive, `Turret` is CW-positive, so every solve aimed the mirror image), VisionPoseCorrector.java:255-269 (Pedro/FTC conversion assumed translation-only when it is a quarter-turn rotation plus a shift — 'every vision correction mapped to a point reflected across the field diagonal - up to ~100 inches wrong'), VisionCorrectedAuto.java:122-133 (raw IMU yaw fed to MegaTag2 instead of field-frame yaw). The frame conversion itself lives as two loose constants: `FIELD_CENTER_OFFSET_INCHES = 72.0` and `PEDRO_TO_FTC_YAW_OFFSET_DEGREES = 90.0`.
painPoints.libraryFix: Types, not comments. Distinct `FieldRelative`/`RobotRelative` wrapper types (or at minimum WPILib `Translation2d`/`Rotation2d`/`ChassisSpeeds` used consistently) so a field-frame error cannot be passed to a robot-frame consumer, plus one `FrameTransform` object owning any external-library conversion with a documented round-trip self-check. The author's own conclusion in AimingCalculator.java:194 — 'Sign conventions at module boundaries deserve as much attention as the math itself' — is the requirement.

painPoints.problem: Manual bulk-cache invalidation is a load-bearing convention with a catastrophic, silent failure mode.
painPoints.evidence: BulkReads.java's own Javadoc: 'forgetting to call clearCache freezes every sensor reading forever, which is the classic bulk-caching bug. Call it first thing in loop().' `BioBuzzCompetition.loop()` line 109 is `BulkReads.clearCache(hubs);` with a comment shouting 'FIRST LINE, every loop'. MANUAL mode was chosen over AUTO deliberately because the codebase reads some encoders more than once per loop — which is itself a consequence of not having a single input-snapshot layer.
painPoints.libraryFix: Own the loop lifecycle in the library so cache invalidation happens in the framework's periodic entry, not the author's first line. The FRC analogue is batched signal refresh (`BaseStatusSignal.refreshAll`) and AdvantageKit's `updateInputs` — a shared `RobotLoop` that begins each cycle by refreshing all registered inputs removes an entire class of stale-sensor bug from user code.

painPoints.problem: Pure, trivially testable logic has zero tests, so every defect had to be found by review or on hardware.
painPoints.evidence: No test source set exists anywhere in TeamCode/build.gradle. `InterpolatingTable`, `AimingCalculator.wrapDegrees`/`solve`, `AllianceFlipUtil.applyX/applyY/applyHeading`, `AutoAlign.driveToPose`, `DriverInput.shape/clamp`, and the mecanum mixing math in `MecanumDrive.drive` are all pure functions with no hardware dependency. Every one of the sign-convention bugs listed above would have been caught by a three-line assertion; instead readme.md's closing line reads 'It compiles ≠ it works ... The whole project compiled cleanly while every single Pedro Pathing autonomous crashed on startup.'
painPoints.libraryFix: Keep the library's math layer hardware-free and ship it with tests, so consumers inherit verified kinematics, angle wrapping, alliance mirroring and interpolation instead of retyping them. The frame-crossing conventions in particular should be pinned by tests (e.g. 'at heading +90, pushing forward strafes robot-right') — the author already wrote exactly that sanity check as a comment in MecanumDrive.java:316-318 but had no place to execute it.

painPoints.problem: Global mutable static state for alliance and robot pose.
painPoints.evidence: `AllianceFlipUtil` holds `private static boolean isRedAlliance` mutated by a static setter (AllianceFlipUtil.java:73-83) and read by static `applyX/applyY/applyHeading`. `RobotState` is a `synchronized` singleton (`getInstance()`, RobotState.java:56-66) holding position and computed velocity; its own Javadoc concedes 'Singletons are worth using sparingly - shared mutable state makes code harder to follow and harder to test.' `Superstructure` separately keeps its own `isBlueAlliance` field, so alliance is stored in two places that can disagree. `SafeHardware.missingDevices` is likewise static, which caused the reset-ordering bug documented at Superstructure.java:108-114.
painPoints.libraryFix: Make alliance an injected value resolved once at init (FRC has `DriverStation.getAlliance()` as the authoritative source) and make pose an explicitly-owned object passed to consumers, or at minimum a single source of truth. The FTC code already pays for the duplication — alliance lives in both `AllianceFlipUtil` and `Superstructure` with no link between them.

painPoints.problem: Servo motion completion is estimated from a timer because FTC servos give no feedback, and this estimate silently participates in the shot interlock.
painPoints.evidence: Hood.java records `lastMoveFraction = Math.abs(clamped - hoodServo.getPosition())` and resets `moveTimer` on every command, then `isAtTarget()` compares elapsed time against `HoodConstants.FULL_TRAVEL_SECONDS = 0.6` scaled by that fraction; Intake.java does the identical thing for its pivot with `PIVOT_TRAVEL_SECONDS = 0.5`. `Superstructure.applyMode()` SHOOTING branch gates firing on `hood.isAtTarget()` — an estimate, not a measurement. Note `hoodServo.getPosition()` returns the last *commanded* position, so the 'current' position it diffs against is itself an assumption.
painPoints.libraryFix: FRC mostly avoids this (servos are rare, and actuators have encoders), so the transferable piece is narrow but real: a `MotionEstimate` type that reports `isAtTarget()` together with its confidence source (measured vs. timed), so an interlock can distinguish 'the hood has arrived' from 'the hood has probably arrived' and a library can refuse to let an estimate silently gate a safety-critical action.

painPoints.problem: Constants organization does not scale past one robot: a single 1156-line file, alphabet-soup naming for variant hardware, and dead sections left in place.
painPoints.evidence: RobotConstants.java holds 13 nested classes in one file. `ShooterConstants` alone spans lines 902-1155 and carries names for all five shooter variants simultaneously (`PARALLEL_LEFT_FLYWHEEL_NAME`, `ROLLER_MOTOR_2_NAME`, `TOWER_A_FEED_NAME`, `TOWER_AGITATOR_NAME`...) even though readme.md says 'build one, delete the rest'. `LauncherConstants` (lines 276-306) is a stale duplicate of `ShooterConstants` with its own `LAUNCHER_MOTOR_NAME`/`FEEDER_SERVO_NAME`/`RPM_CLOSE`/`RPM_FAR` and appears unused by any mechanism. `ShooterConstants` also declares `HOOD_SERVO_NAME` while a separate `HoodConstants` declares `HOOD_SERVO_NAME` again — two sources for the same device.
painPoints.libraryFix: Per-mechanism config objects constructed and passed in (rather than statically reached into), so a robot declares only the mechanisms it has and a variant that isn't built has no constants at all. This also kills the duplicate-name problem structurally: a device name exists once, in the config handed to the mechanism that owns it.

source: C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/0000-XXXX-Robot-Template (76 Java files, ~9.6k LOC incl. 1946-line vendored LimelightHelpers; git history: 3 commits, "Initial commit" + a Fable-5 code-review fix pass)
summary: This is a dense, opinionated, genuinely good template — not vendor boilerplate. It is deliberately STATE-BASED, not command-based: subsystems are plain actuator classes (no SubsystemBase, no Commands, no Triggers), a single `Superstructure` state machine drives every mechanism from a 12-value `SuperState` enum, and `RobotContainer` polls `XboxController` directly. WPILib's CommandScheduler runs only for the two external tools that require it (PathPlanner autos/pathfinding and SysId). Every mechanism AND the swerve drivetrain sit behind a hand-rolled AdvantageKit IO trio (`XxxIO` interface with an `@AutoLog XxxIOInputs` inner class + default no-op methods, `XxxIOTalonFX` that also hosts the physics sim, `XxxIONeo`, and an anonymous `new XxxIO(){}` for REPLAY), so the whole robot replays deterministically; 10 mechanisms + swerve = ~14 `Logger.processInputs` sites and ~10 near-identical TalonFX config blocks. Everything — CAN IDs, gear ratios, gains, presets, soft limits, sim masses, vision config, logging indices — lives in ONE 712-line `Constants.java` of nested `static final class` sections annotated with a hand-rolled `ADD` / `VERIFY` / `TUNE` marker convention and a unit in every trailing comment. The single biggest cost is per-mechanism copy-paste: the same `TalonFXConfiguration` + cached-StatusSignal + `optimizeBusUtilization` + sim-advance block, the same `private enum ControlMode {POSITION, DUTY_CYCLE, NEUTRAL}` (5 verbatim copies), the same clamp/`setManual`/`holdCurrentX`/`isAtTarget` bodies, the same `/ 360.0` degree↔rotation conversion inlined 41 times, and a 9-line nested-ternary IO selector in RobotContainer. Tuning is 100% redeploy-based — every gain is a compile-time `static final`, no IO exposes a `setGains`, and the author's own `LoggedTunableNumber`/`LoggedTunableBoolean` are never called anywhere in the repo (alongside `GeomUtil`, `EqualsUtil`, `AutoAlign`, and a `RobotState` singleton that is written but never read).

Vendordeps: AdvantageKit 26.0.2 (+ `akit-autolog` annotationProcessor whose version is parsed out of `vendordeps/AdvantageKit.json` at build time by a JsonSlurper in build.gradle so it can't drift), CTRE Phoenix 6 v26.3.0, REVLib 2026.0.5, PathplannerLib 2026.1.2, photonlib v2026.2.2, WPILib-New-Commands 1.0.0. patterns.name: AdvantageKit IO trio (interface + @AutoLog inputs + no-op default methods)
patterns.whatItDoes: Every mechanism package is `XxxIO.java` (interface holding an `@AutoLog class XxxIOInputs` POJO of everything read FROM hardware, plus `default void` no-op output methods), `XxxIOTalonFX.java` (real hardware AND physics sim in one class), `XxxIONeo.java`, and `Xxx.java` (the subsystem, which calls `io.updateInputs(inputs); Logger.processInputs("Arm", inputs);` then makes every decision from `inputs`, never from hardware). REPLAY passes an anonymous `new ArmIO(){}` so all inputs come from the log.
patterns.whereSeen: C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/0000-XXXX-Robot-Template/src/main/java/frc/robot/subsystems/arm/ArmIO.java (canonical, most-documented copy — other IOs literally say "See {@code arm.ArmIO} for the pattern"); repeated for elevator, wrist, turret, shooter, intake, indexer, endeffector, climber, vision, swerve/ModuleIO, swerve/GyroIO
patterns.libraryValue: This is the single most-repeated structure in the repo (11 copies). PumpkinLib should ship the inputs struct + the subsystem shell as generics/base classes (`PositionMechanism`, `VelocityMechanism`, `RollerMechanism`) so a team writes only the hardware-specific config, not the 40-line ceremony. The `default {}` no-op convention for the REPLAY IO is the exact right primitive to keep.

patterns.name: Three-mode IO selection driven by one `Mode` enum
patterns.whatItDoes: `Constants.LoggingConstants.getMode()` returns `RobotBase.isReal() ? REAL : SIM_MODE` where `SIM_MODE` is a hand-edited constant (SIM or REPLAY). RobotContainer then builds each subsystem's IO from that mode crossed with a per-mechanism `MOTOR_TYPE` constant.
patterns.whereSeen: Constants.java lines 683-711 (LoggingConstants, Mode enum, getMode()); RobotContainer.java lines 137-218; Robot.java lines 42-64 (logger receivers per mode)
patterns.libraryValue: The intent ("one constant swaps motor family; one enum swaps REAL/SIM/REPLAY") is excellent; the expression of it is nine copies of a nested ternary that is trivially easy to typo. A library should own this as `IOFactory.select(mode, motorType, krakenSupplier, neoSupplier, simSupplier)` or an annotation/registry, and it should also fix the current wart that SIM silently ignores MOTOR_TYPE (the NEO IOs have no sim at all).

patterns.name: Single-file Constants with unit comments, ADD/VERIFY/TUNE markers, and a CAN ID map header
patterns.whatItDoes: One 712-line `Constants.java`, nested `public static final class XxxConstants` per subsystem, private ctor on the outer class. Every value carries its unit in a trailing comment and a marker: TUNE (a gain to dial in), VERIFY (a physical measurement), ADD (something you must supply). The file header contains a hand-maintained ASCII CAN ID map (1=Pigeon, 2/3/4=FL drive/steer/cancoder, ... 26=EndEffector) and a conventions block explaining that Phoenix 6 gains are voltage-based with error in mechanism rotations.
patterns.whereSeen: C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/0000-XXXX-Robot-Template/src/main/java/frc/robot/Constants.java (whole file); markers appear ~90 times
patterns.libraryValue: The ADD/VERIFY/TUNE taxonomy is a real, reusable idea — a library could formalize it as annotations or a config record with required/measured/tunable fields, and generate a first-setup checklist or a startup Alert for anything still at its placeholder. The derived-constant style (`INCHES_PER_DRUM_ROTATION = circumference * stages`) is exactly the shape a `LinearMechanismGeometry` value type should take.

patterns.name: Preset enums carrying a unit-typed payload
patterns.whatItDoes: Setpoints are not loose doubles; each mechanism declares a nested `enum Preset` whose constants hold a value and expose it through a unit-named accessor, and the subsystem takes the enum directly.
patterns.whereSeen: Constants.java ElevatorConstants.Preset (lines 282-287), ArmConstants.Preset (334-339), WristConstants.Preset (380-385); consumed in Elevator.setGoal / Arm.setGoal / Wrist.setGoal and Superstructure.stowElevatorArmWrist()

A library should generalize it to a `Setpoint<Distance>` / `Setpoint<Angle>` (or WPILib Units `Measure`) so presets, soft limits, and tolerances all share one unit-checked type instead of bare doubles.

patterns.name: Superstructure state machine with an on-entry latch
patterns.whatItDoes: A 12-state enum (`IDLE, INTAKE, HOLD, EJECT, AIM, SHOOT, SCORE_LOW/MID/HIGH, CLIMB_DEPLOY, CLIMB, MANUAL`); `periodic()` computes `boolean onEntry = state != prevState` then calls `applyState(state, onEntry)`, a giant switch that pushes setpoints to every mechanism every loop. `resetStateEntry()` re-arms the latch on disable so IDLE's entry action (capturing the climber hold position) fires again.
patterns.whereSeen: C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/0000-XXXX-Robot-Template/src/main/java/frc/robot/Superstructure.java lines 130-246; resetStateEntry called from RobotContainer.setDisabled() line 448
patterns.libraryValue: The onEntry latch + the disable-time re-arm is a subtle, hard-won detail worth owning in a library (`StateMachine<S>` with onEnter/whileIn/onExit hooks). It would also kill the current footgun where every case must remember to zero every actuator (see pain points).

patterns.name: Hand-rolled AdvantageKit-native swerve (GyroIO + 4 ModuleIO + PhoenixOdometryThread)
patterns.whatItDoes: Deliberately replaces CTRE's SwerveDrivetrain wrapper so the drivetrain replays. `Swerve` owns a `GyroIO` + four `Module`s, WPILib `SwerveDriveKinematics` + `SwerveDrivePoseEstimator`, feeds EVERY high-frequency odometry sample into the estimator, falls back to twist-integrated heading when the gyro is absent, caches measured states/speeds once per loop, and exposes SysId. `PhoenixOdometryThread` is a singleton daemon thread that `waitForAll`s on CAN FD or polls at ODOMETRY_FREQUENCY_HZ on the rio bus, with a `ReentrantLock odometryLock` that Swerve holds while draining.

patterns.name: Single-source swerve gains in physical units, converted per-controller inside each IO
patterns.whatItDoes: DRIVE_kS/kV/kA/kP and TURN_kP/kD are declared once in VOLTS per WHEEL RADIAN(/s). ModuleIOTalonFX multiplies by 2π (its loop runs in wheel rotations via SensorToMechanismRatio); ModuleIONeo divides by 12 (voltage-compensated duty-cycle loop). A unit test pins the invariant.

painPoints.problem: Live tuning is impossible — every gain is a compile-time constant, and the author's own tunable classes are dead code
painPoints.evidence: `grep -rn LoggedTunableNumber|LoggedTunableBoolean src/` returns only their own definitions and Javadoc — zero call sites. No IO exposes a `setGains`/`applyGains`; gains are read once in each IO constructor (e.g. ArmIOTalonFX.java:62-67 `config.Slot0.kP = ArmConstants.kP;`). `LoggedTunableNumber`'s own Javadoc says "Use it while dialing in a gain, then paste the final value into Constants" but no mechanism wires it. Same for `GeomUtil`, `EqualsUtil`, `AutoAlign` (never called), and `RobotState` (written by Swerve.java:190, never read).
painPoints.libraryFix: Make tunability the default path: every library mechanism publishes its gains as tunables under `/Tuning/<Subsystem>/kP` in a dev/tuning build, polls `hasChanged()` in periodic, and re-applies via a mandatory `IO.setGains(...)`. Ship a one-flag switch between 'tunable' and 'frozen constants' so the same code compiles for competition.

painPoints.problem: Robot geometry is duplicated between Constants.java and PathPlanner's settings.json and must be kept in sync by hand
painPoints.evidence: Constants.java: `TRACK_WIDTH_METERS = Units.inchesToMeters(24.75)` = 0.62865, `WHEEL_RADIUS_METERS = inchesToMeters(2.0)` = 0.0508, `DRIVE_GEAR_RATIO = 5.357142857142857`, `MAX_LINEAR_SPEED_MPS = 5.96`, `DRIVE_STATOR_CURRENT_LIMIT = 90.0`. deploy/pathplanner/settings.json: `robotTrackwidth: 0.628`, `driveWheelRadius: 0.051`, `driveGearing: 5.36`, `maxDriveSpeed: 5.96`, `driveCurrentLimit: 90.0`, plus module X/Y of ±0.314. Constants.java line 168 says outright "keep settings.json 'maxDriveSpeed' in sync"; README line 337 repeats it. `Swerve.configureAutoBuilder()` then loads `RobotConfig.fromGUISettings()` — so the JSON, not Constants, is what PathPlanner actually believes.
painPoints.libraryFix: Either generate settings.json from the Java config at build/deploy time, or have the library read the JSON as the single source and derive Constants from it — plus a startup consistency check that raises an Alert when the two disagree beyond a tolerance.

painPoints.problem: Every Superstructure state must remember to reset every actuator; forgetting one leaves hardware running
painPoints.evidence: Superstructure.java case MANUAL:220-222 has the comment "Don't leave rollers running at whatever the previous state set." case EJECT:176 has "entering from AIM/SHOOT must spin the flywheels down". The IDLE, INTAKE, HOLD cases each repeat the same four lines (`intake.retract(); intake.setRollerSpeed(0); indexer.stop(); endEffector.stop();`). AIM (183-187) notably does NOT call `intake.retract()` or touch the endEffector — an asymmetry that is invisible until it bites.
painPoints.libraryFix: Invert the model: each loop the library writes DEFAULT outputs for every mechanism, then the active state overrides only what it cares about. That makes 'forgot to stop the roller' structurally impossible and shrinks each case to its actual intent.

painPoints.problem: The NEO path is real code that is never simulated or tested
painPoints.evidence: RobotContainer.java:151-152 comments "SIM: ALWAYS the TalonFX IO - it hosts the physics sim (the NEO IOs have none)"; the ternaries gate on `!sim &&`. No `XxxIONeo` constructs any WPILib sim. Every NEO IO hardcodes `inputs.connected = true` (ArmIONeo:60, ElevatorIONeo:72-73, ShooterIONeo:60-61, TurretIONeo:53, ClimberIONeo:52, IntakeIONeo:67/73, ModuleIONeo:100/106 — "Spark MAX has no cheap connection signal"). TurretIONeo.setAngle:62-64 silently drops the chassis-omega feedforward. ModuleIONeo:114-117 emits one odometry sample per loop from `Timer.getFPGATimestamp()` (not the AKit-deterministic `Timer.getTimestamp()` used elsewhere).
painPoints.libraryFix: Give the library's REV backend the same sim support and a real connection/fault check (Spark `getFaults`/`getStickyFaults` or a warning-counter heartbeat), and unify the timestamp source. Otherwise the 'switch one constant to NEO' promise ships untested code to a competition.

painPoints.problem: Wrist manual control hardcodes magic numbers because WristConstants lacks the fields every sibling has
painPoints.evidence: Wrist.java:50-51 — `if (Math.abs(stickInput) >= 0.1) { manualOutput = stickInput * 0.15; }`. Every other mechanism uses named constants (`ArmConstants.MANUAL_DEADBAND`, `MANUAL_SPEED_LIMIT`, etc.), but Constants.WristConstants (lines 356-390) defines no MANUAL_* fields at all. Also, `Wrist.setManual`, `Turret.setManual`, `Climber.setManual`, `Elevator.resetEncoder()`, and `Climber.retractFully()` are never called from anywhere — Superstructure MANUAL only drives elevator + arm.
painPoints.libraryFix: A shared mechanism config record with required manual-control fields makes the omission a compile error rather than a silently different feel on one joint. Dead setters disappear once manual control is a library feature toggled per mechanism.

painPoints.problem: Boot position seeding trusts that mechanisms are parked at a known hard stop, with no absolute encoder anywhere
painPoints.evidence: ArmIOTalonFX.java:76 `motor.setPosition(ArmConstants.START_ANGLE / 360.0);`, WristIOTalonFX:66, IntakeIOTalonFX:48, TurretIOTalonFX:62 `motor.setPosition(0)`, ClimberIOTalonFX:60, ElevatorIOTalonFX:83-84. Constants.java:324 states the assumption: "The arm is seeded to START_ANGLE at boot (assumes it rests on a known hard stop)." Sensors.java sections 6 and 7 document how to add a Through Bore / CANcoder to fix this, but nothing is wired — and the fused-CANcoder pattern is only used in ModuleIOTalonFX.
painPoints.libraryFix: Ship first-class homing strategies (absolute-encoder seed, current-limit homing, limit-switch homing) as a pluggable `ZeroingStrategy` on every position mechanism, with the fused-CANcoder config already correct.

painPoints.problem: Alerts/errors go to places nobody watches, and only two alerts exist for a 10-mechanism robot
painPoints.evidence: PhoenixUtil.java:27 prints a config failure to `System.err`. Swerve.java:124 and RobotContainer.java:367/397 use `DriverStation.reportError`. Dashboard.java:116-119 defines exactly two WPILib `Alert`s (low battery, elevator sides out of sync) — despite every IO already logging a `connected` boolean and a `temperatureCelsius` that nothing consumes.
painPoints.libraryFix: A `HealthMonitor` that auto-registers an Alert per device from the IO inputs the library already collects (disconnected, over-temp, config-apply failure, follower disagreement, CAN utilization) — zero per-robot wiring.

painPoints.problem: A few smaller correctness/consistency traps worth designing out
painPoints.evidence: (a) `SwerveConstants.MAX_ANGULAR_SPEED_RAD_PER_SEC` is derived from track width but the driver also multiplies by `ROTATION_SPEED_SCALE` in RobotContainer:255 while translation uses `DRIVE_SPEED_SCALE` — two unrelated scalars with no shared clamp. (b) Constants.ArmConstants.SIM_SIMULATE_GRAVITY = false and kG = 0.0 with the comment that Arm_Cosine "is only correct when 0 deg = arm horizontal" — a real convention landmine left to the user. (c) `Swerve.addVisionMeasurement` reaches for a fully-qualified `frc.robot.Constants.VisionConstants.MAX_ANGULAR_SPEED_FOR_VISION` (line 282) instead of importing, a hint the vision gate lives in the wrong layer. (d) ModuleIOTalonFX/ModuleIONeo/GyroIOPigeon2 apply configs WITHOUT `PhoenixUtil.tryUntilOk`, unlike all 10 mechanism IOs. (e) `Vision.stdDevs` uses a literal `9999999` sentinel for 'don't trust heading' (Vision.java:87) and a magic `1.0 + d*d/30.0` distance scale (line 82).
painPoints.libraryFix: Own the angle-convention contract (declare where zero is and whether gravity is cosine- or static-type, and derive the Phoenix GravityType from it), make retrying config application the only code path, and express vision trust as a named, tunable `TrustModel` instead of sentinels and inline polynomials.

constraints: WPILib 2026 / GradleRIO 2026.2.1 and Java 17 exactly (build.gradle sets sourceCompatibility/targetCompatibility VERSION_17; gradle.properties pins org.gradle.java.home to the WPILib JDK because a foreign JAVA_HOME hard-crashes test JVMs loading wpiHal). PumpkinLib must compile on Java 17 — no Java 21 features.

AdvantageKit deterministic replay is non-negotiable and shapes every API: anything read from hardware MUST pass through an @AutoLog inputs struct, subsystems must decide only from `inputs`, and time must come from `Timer.getTimestamp()` not `Timer.getFPGATimestamp()` (explicitly called out in Superstructure.java:85-87 and Vision.java:73-75). Any library abstraction that hides a direct hardware read breaks replay and will be rejected.

AdvantageKit's `@AutoLog` annotation processor generates `XxxIOInputsAutoLogged` from a class in the user's source tree; the akit-autolog version is pulled out of vendordeps/AdvantageKit.json at build time. A library shipping pre-generated or generic input structs must not fight this processor, and AutoLogOutputManager only discovers `@AutoLogOutput` fields reachable from the robot object graph AND inside the `frc.robot` package — a `pumpkinlib.*` package will NOT be auto-scanned unless the library handles registration itself.

State-based, not command-based. No mechanism may be a Command/SubsystemBase/Trigger. `Swerve implements Subsystem` only so SysId and PathPlanner can `require` it; the CommandScheduler is allowed to run ONLY PathPlanner autos/pathfinding, SysId, and PathPlanner warmup. A command-factory-first library API would be rejected outright.

Every mechanism and the swerve modules must support BOTH Kraken X60/TalonFX (Phoenix 6 v26.3.0) and NEO/Spark MAX (REVLib 2026.0.5), switchable by exactly one constant, sharing one set of CAN IDs, offsets, and physically-expressed gains.

Vision must remain backend-swappable between Limelight (vendored LimelightHelpers, MegaTag1 while disabled / MegaTag2 while enabled) and PhotonVision (photonlib v2026.2.2) behind a single constant, producing identical logged observation arrays.

Autonomous is PathPlannerLib 2026.1.2 + Choreo `.traj` through the same chooser, with `Pathfinding.setPathfinder(new LocalADStarAK())` and `RobotConfig.fromGUISettings()` — so deploy/pathplanner/settings.json remains an external source of truth the library must reconcile with, not replace.

The project must build, `./gradlew test`, and `simulateJava` out of the box with placeholder values and team number 0 — a library that requires real CAN IDs or measured constants before it compiles breaks the template's core promise.

Unit tests fork one JVM per class (`forkEvery = 1`) because simulated CAN devices reject duplicate IDs in a process, and AdvantageKit's Logger cannot restart within a JVM (AutoLogOutputTest must stay single-@Test). Any library test helpers must respect both limits.

The one-file `Constants.java` is a deliberate, documented design decision ("THE ONE AND ONLY CONSTANTS FILE"), as is the ADD/VERIFY/TUNE marker convention and a unit in every trailing comment. A library that scatters configuration across many files, or replaces it with YAML/JSON, works against the author's stated intent.

Style to match: 4-space indent, ALL_CAPS_SNAKE constants EXCEPT gains which are literally `kP, kI, kD, kS, kV, kG`; units baked into identifiers (`_METERS`, `_INCHES`, `Deg`, `RadPerSec`, `Rps`, `Amps`, `Celsius`); human units (inches/degrees) at the API boundary with rotations confined inside the IO; `record`s for value types (ModuleConfig, ShotParameters); enums-with-payload for presets; one-line method bodies for trivial overrides (`@Override public void setNeutral() { motor.setControl(neutralRequest); }`); a teaching-grade Javadoc block on EVERY class explaining WHY; no `m_` prefixes outside the WPILib-generated Robot.java; ASCII only, no emoji.

No CLAUDE.md exists in this repo; .claude/settings.local.json contains only a single Bash permission entry. There is no project-specific agent guidance to conform to beyond the README (487 lines) and the in-code Javadoc.

source: C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/9143-2025-A-Updated and C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/9143-2025-B-Updated (FRC team 9143, two sibling 2025 Reefscape robots, both updated to 2026 deps)
summary: These are two well-written, heavily-commented, plain-WPILib command-based robots (no AdvantageKit IO layers, no replay) that share an enormous amount of literally copy-pasted infrastructure. Swerve.java (500 lines) is byte-identical between the two robots except for ONE comment line; Telemetry.java, LimelightHelpers.java (1946 lines), util/Elastic.java (390 lines), Main.java, build.gradle, gradle.properties, .vscode/settings.json, RobotContainerTest.java and ChoreoTrajectoryTest.java are all 100% identical; Vision.java differs only in the goal-resolver body; Robot.java differs by 19 lines (mostly the log metadata string); RobotContainer.java shares ~180 identical lines of drive requests, D-pad nudges, SysId bindings, Choreo auto discovery, and vision toggle. Architecture is: one god `Constants.java` of nested `public static final class XConstants` with a hand-maintained CAN ID map in the header comment, CTRE Tuner-X-generated `TunerConstants.java` for swerve, subsystems that own hardware directly and expose plain getters, a central `Dashboard.java` that is the *only* NetworkTables publisher, and (in A only) a `Superstructure.java` command-factory motion planner with collision interlocks. Every gain, limit, preset, and sim constant is a hardcoded `public static final double` — there is not a single tunable number, `Preferences` call, or `SmartDashboard.getNumber` anywhere in either repo; tuning is done by editing Java and redeploying, or via REV Hardware Client / Tuner X. Simulation is hand-wired per subsystem (`ElevatorSim`, `SingleJointedArmSim`, `SparkMaxSim`, TalonFX `getSimState()`) with the same ~15-line `simulationPeriodic()` shape repeated. Logging is AdvantageKit `LoggedRobot` + `WPILOGWriter` + `RLOGServer(5810)` with all `Logger.recordOutput` calls funneled through `Dashboard.update()`. The repos are NOT thin and are NOT vendor boilerplate — they represent a mature, opinionated house style with real hard-won knowledge (FPGA→Phoenix timestamp conversion, MegaTag1-while-disabled heading seeding, non-blocking `setPosition(x, 0)`, spin-based vision rejection) that is currently trapped in copy-paste.
stack: WPILib 2026 / GradleRIO 2026.2.1, Java 17 (`sourceCompatibility = JavaVersion.VERSION_17`), Gradle pinned to `org.gradle.java.home=C:/Users/Public/wpilib/2026/jdk` via gradle.properties. Vendordeps (identical version-for-version in both repos): Phoenix6 26.3.0, REVLib 2026.0.5, PathplannerLib 2026.1.2, AdvantageKit 26.0.2, WPILibNewCommands 1.0.0. LimelightHelpers v1.14 vendored as source (requires LLOS 2026.0+). Elastic dashboard via vendored `util/Elastic.java` (Gold87 ElasticLib) + `deploy/elastic-layout.json` served over `WebServer.start(5800, ...)`. Motor controllers: Kraken X60 / TalonFX (swerve drive+steer, A's CorAl pivot+intake), NEO on Spark MAX (A's elevator x2, B's KitBot roller, B's AlLow pivot+roller). Sensors: CANcoder x4, Pigeon 2 (id 2), CTRE CANrange (A, game piece), REV Through Bore absolute encoder on DIO 0 (A, pivot), CTRE CANdle (A, LEDs, id 5), 3x Limelight (A: funnel/barge/reef; B: zero cameras, stack inert). Autonomous: PathPlanner AutoBuilder + Choreo `.traj` loaded through `PathPlannerPath.fromChoreoTrajectory` (ChoreoLib deliberately NOT used - no 2026 release). Testing: JUnit 5 (5.10.1) with `forkEvery = 1` because simulated CAN devices reject duplicate IDs in one JVM. NOTE: `settings.gradle` disagrees between repos — A has `String frcYear = '2025'`, B has `'2026'`, while both `.wpilib/wpilib_preferences.json` say `"projectYear": "2026"`.

patterns.name: Swerve subsystem wrapper over CTRE TunerSwerveDrivetrain (THE strongest duplication signal)
patterns.whatItDoes: Extends the Tuner-X-generated `TunerSwerveDrivetrain` and implements `Subsystem`, layering on: three duplicated constructors that each repeat `new Vision(this)` + `startSimThread()` + `createAprilTagTrackingCommand()` + `configureAutoBuilder()`; PathPlanner AutoBuilder wiring with `RobotConfig.fromGUISettings()` in a try/catch; `applyRequest(Supplier<SwerveRequest>)`; three SysId routines (translation/steer/rotation) with a `setSysIdRoutine(SysIdRoutineType)` selector; alliance-aware operator perspective in `periodic()`; a 5 ms `Notifier` sim thread; and an overridden `addVisionMeasurement` doing FPGA→Phoenix timebase conversion plus spin-based rejection.
patterns.whereSeen: C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/9143-2025-A-Updated/src/main/java/frc/robot/subsystems/Swerve.java (500 lines) and C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/9143-2025-B-Updated/src/main/java/frc/robot/subsystems/Swerve.java (499 lines) — `diff --strip-trailing-cr` reports exactly 3 differing lines, all inside one Javadoc sentence.
patterns.libraryValue: This is 500 lines of nontrivial, correctness-critical code duplicated verbatim across two robots. It should be PumpkinLib's flagship class: a `PumpkinSwerve` base that takes drivetrain constants + a path-following gain record + a vision-goal strategy, exposing the SysId routines, AutoBuilder config, operator perspective, and the timestamp/spin-rejection logic for free. The two robot-specific deltas (auto PID gains, vision goal resolver) are exactly the injection points.

patterns.name: Centralized Dashboard publisher (subsystems publish nothing)
patterns.whatItDoes: A single non-Subsystem `Dashboard` class constructed in RobotContainer and pumped once per loop from `Robot.robotPeriodic()` via `m_robotContainer.updateDashboard()`. It owns: `Field2d`, the Elastic `SwerveDrive` widget (raw NT subtable with a `.type` marker and 9 cached `NetworkTableEntry`s), `Mechanism2d` schematics, `Pose3d[]` component poses for AdvantageScope, every `SmartDashboard.putX` call, every `Logger.recordOutput` call, and every WPILib `Alert`. Every subsystem carries the identical Javadoc line: "Dashboard note: this subsystem publishes nothing itself."
patterns.whereSeen: A: .../frc/robot/Dashboard.java (332 lines); B: .../frc/robot/Dashboard.java (235 lines). ~90 lines are character-identical (swerve widget setup, vitals block, alliance/battery alert, vision block).
patterns.libraryValue: The *shape* is excellent and should be preserved, but the mechanical parts are pure boilerplate: the Elastic SwerveDrive widget setup, the drivetrain vitals block (Speed/Heading/Match Time/Battery/CAN Utilization), the low-battery alert, and the vision has-target key precomputation are identical. PumpkinLib should ship `PumpkinDashboard` with pluggable "panels" so a robot only writes its own mechanism block, plus a declarative `Alert` helper (condition supplier + message + one-shot Elastic toast on rising edge) — A hand-rolls that toast latch with a `throughBoreWasConnected` boolean.

patterns.name: Choreo-trajectory auto discovery folded into the PathPlanner chooser
patterns.whatItDoes: `addChoreoAutos()` scans `Filesystem.getDeployDirectory()/choreo` for `*.traj`, sorts them, loads each via `PathPlannerPath.fromChoreoTrajectory(name)`, and adds it to the same `LoggedDashboardChooser` as `"Choreo: <name>"`. `choreoAutoCommand(path)` resets odometry to the trajectory's start pose, alliance-flipping it with `AutoBuilder.shouldFlip() ? FlippingUtil.flipFieldPose(start) : start`, then follows. A malformed file is reported via `DriverStation.reportError` and skipped rather than crashing construction.
patterns.whereSeen: A: RobotContainer.java lines 335-367; B: RobotContainer.java lines 308-340. Byte-identical including the 15-line Javadoc explaining why ChoreoLib is not used.
patterns.libraryValue: Genuinely reusable, non-obvious, and already battle-tested (there's a dedicated `ChoreoTrajectoryTest` in both repos, also identical). Should be a one-liner in PumpkinLib: `PumpkinAuto.addChoreoTrajectories(chooser, drivetrain)`.

patterns.name: Multi-Limelight MegaTag1/MegaTag2 pose fusion with disabled-time heading seeding
patterns.whatItDoes: Per loop: pushes gyro heading to every camera with `SetRobotOrientation_NoFlush` (one `LimelightHelpers.Flush()` after the loop instead of per-camera), then chooses MegaTag1 while DISABLED (so its absolute heading solve seeds the gyro) and MegaTag2 while enabled. Std devs are computed as `xyStdDev = 0.3 + 0.4*avgTagDist^2 / max(1, tagCount)` and `rotStdDev = disabled ? (tagCount>=2 ? 0.3 : 0.9) : 9999999`. Also caches a `findBestTarget()` result once per `periodic()` so dashboard + tracking command share one NT read.
patterns.whereSeen: A: subsystems/Vision.java lines 320-363; B: subsystems/Vision.java (same block, character-identical). The whole `updateRobotPosition()` method, the `AprilTagTarget`/`TrackingGoal` value classes, `isReefTag`/`isCoralStationTag` linear scans, `toggleTracking`, `hasTarget(int)`, and the precomputed `limelightTableNames` array are all duplicated.
patterns.libraryValue: This is the single hardest-to-get-right piece of FRC vision code and it is copy-pasted. PumpkinLib should own it as `PumpkinVision`: a camera list (name + facing sign), a std-dev policy interface, and the MegaTag1-while-disabled seeding baked in. Only the goal resolver differs between robots (A resolves per superstructure goal + branch side; B returns flush-and-centered), which is exactly a strategy/functional-interface seam.

patterns.name: "Positional mechanism with latched setpoint + manual override that holds on release"
patterns.whatItDoes: The same subsystem skeleton appears three times across the two repos (A's Elevator on Spark MAX MAXMotion, A's CorAl pivot on TalonFX Motion Magic, B's AlLow pivot on Spark MAX position control). Every one has: `private double target; private boolean manualModeEnabled; private boolean positionControlEnabled;`, a `setPosition/setPivotAngle` that clamps to MIN/MAX and flips the two booleans, a `holdCurrentPosition()/holdCurrentAngle()` that calls set(get()), a `manualControl(stick)` that applies a deadband + speed limit and captures-and-holds on release, an `isAtTarget()` using an ALLOWED_ERROR constant, a `stopX()` that drops the closed loop, a `resetEncoder()`, and 4 diagnostic getters (`getXCurrent`, `getXOutput`).
patterns.whereSeen: A/.../subsystems/Elevator.java (lines 56-60, 170-219, 226-276), A/.../subsystems/CorAl.java (lines 65-68, 190-280), B/.../subsystems/AlLow.java (lines 60-65, 183-291).
patterns.libraryValue: This is the highest-leverage mechanism abstraction in the codebase. PumpkinLib should provide a `PositionMechanism` base (or a composable `SetpointHolder` + `ManualOverride` pair) parameterized by a motor-controller adapter, so a new elevator/arm/pivot is ~30 lines of config instead of ~250 lines of near-identical state machine. The three-boolean state (`manualModeEnabled` / `positionControlEnabled` / implicit "neither") is exactly the kind of hand-rolled state that a library enum should own.

patterns.name: Superstructure: deferred, state-gated collision-avoidance motion planner (A only)
patterns.whatItDoes: A non-Subsystem command factory that owns ALL coordinated elevator+arm motion. `moveTo()` wraps `Commands.defer(() -> planMove(h, a), Set.of(elevator, coral))` so the plan is built from REAL mechanism state at button-press time. `planMove` has three cases (low-box direct / tuck-from-low-box / general), and the general path is `escapeCurrentPose(...).andThen(travelAndFinish(...))`. Overlaps are gated on measured position (`Commands.waitUntil(() -> elevator.getCurrentPosition() >= handoff)`), never on timing. The ascending escape re-evaluates its ceiling every loop so the elevator target ratchets up as the arm swings, avoiding stop-and-go stutter. A `Goal` enum records the last commanded pose family and is handed to Vision via `swerve.getVision().setGoalSupplier(superstructure::getGoal)`.
patterns.whereSeen: C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/9143-2025-A-Updated/src/main/java/frc/robot/Superstructure.java (449 lines). No equivalent in B.
patterns.libraryValue: Not directly shareable (the geometry is robot-specific), but the *pattern* absolutely is: deferred planning from live state, measured-state gates rather than timeouts, a `settle()` helper with a timeout on the final wait only, and `handleInterrupt(stopRollers)` on every roller command. PumpkinLib should ship the scaffolding — a `Superstructure<G extends Enum<G>>` base with `defer`-based `moveTo`, a `settle(timeout)` helper, and a goal-enum → vision-goal supplier bridge — plus a documented "safe region" declaration API so teams describe forbidden (height, angle) zones instead of hand-writing the branch tree.

patterns.name: Preset enum with a single `double` payload
patterns.whatItDoes: Every mechanism's setpoints are a nested enum carrying one primitive: `PresetHeights.CORAL_L4(52.5).getHeight()`, `PivotPresetAngles.RAISE(90.0).getAngle()`, B's `AlLowConstants.PivotPresetAngles.INTAKE(45.0).getAngle()`. Each enum re-declares the same private field + constructor + getter boilerplate.
patterns.whereSeen: A/Constants.java lines 120-139 (PresetHeights) and 232-257 (PivotPresetAngles); B/Constants.java lines 119-133 (PivotPresetAngles).
patterns.libraryValue: The idea is right (named, self-documenting setpoints beat magic numbers at call sites), but the 8-line boilerplate is re-typed per enum, the getters have inconsistent names (`getHeight` vs `getAngle`), and the values are raw doubles with the unit only in a comment. PumpkinLib should offer a `Setpoint` interface (`double value()`) or unit-typed presets (`Distance`/`Angle` from `edu.wpi.first.units`) so presets are dimension-checked — the author already imports `edu.wpi.first.units.Units.*` in TunerConstants and clearly likes units.

patterns.name: Derived-gearing constants written as visible tooth-count arithmetic
patterns.whatItDoes: Gear ratios are never written as a magic decimal; they are written as the multiplication of real tooth counts with the power path spelled out in the comment above. This is the single best habit in the codebase.
patterns.whereSeen: A/Constants.java line 59 `ELEVATOR_GEAR_RATIO = 5.0 * 3.0 * 3.0`, line 64 `ELEVATOR_SPROCKET_CIRCUMFERENCE = 22 * 0.25`, line 74 `ELEVATOR_INCHES_PER_ROTATION = SPROCKET_CIRCUMFERENCE * CASCADE_RATIO / GEAR_RATIO`, line 173 `CORAL_PIVOT_GEAR_RATIO = (58.0/10.0) * (58.0/18.0) * (42.0/12.0)`; A/TunerConstants.java line 107 `kCoupleRatio = 50.0 / 16.0`.
patterns.libraryValue: PumpkinLib should formalize this as a tiny `Gearing`/`Reduction` builder (`Reduction.of(58,10).then(58,18).then(42,12)` → `.ratio()`), plus `Conversions` helpers for sprocket-pitch-to-linear and cascade multipliers. It makes the good habit cheap and makes the derivation machine-checkable rather than comment-checkable. Contrast with B's AlLow, where the author had to *reverse-engineer* the ratio: `ALLOW_PIVOT_POSITION_CONVERSION = 13.334; // 13.334 deg/rot implies a ~27:1 reduction (360 / 13.334). VERIFY` — exactly the failure this abstraction prevents.

patterns.name: KitBot command-factory subsystem (startEnd + withTimeout + withName)
patterns.whatItDoes: A roller subsystem that exposes ONLY command factories, never raw setters. Each is `startEnd(() -> motor.set(SPEED), motor::stopMotor).withTimeout(D).withName("X")`. The same factories are consumed by both button bindings and PathPlanner `NamedCommands.registerCommand(...)`, so there is exactly one definition of "eject".
patterns.whereSeen: B/.../subsystems/KitBot.java lines 55-86; registered in B/RobotContainer.java lines 118-121.
patterns.libraryValue: This is the cleanest subsystem in either repo and the pattern the others should follow (A's CorAl exposes raw `setIntakeSpeed` and the Superstructure must manually add `.handleInterrupt(coral::stopIntake)` to four separate commands). PumpkinLib should ship a `RollerSubsystem` with `runAt(speed)`, `runFor(speed, duration)`, and automatic stop-on-end, plus a helper that registers a map of NamedCommands so the string names can't drift from the .auto files.

patterns.name: State-derived LED subsystem with change-detection (A only)
patterns.whatItDoes: A CANdle subsystem driven entirely by `BooleanSupplier`s injected at construction (`new LEDs(coral::isGamePieceDetected, swerve::isVisionTrackingEnabled)`). `computeState()` returns an `LEDState` from a fixed priority ladder; `periodic()` only calls `applyState()` when the state changes OR when the alliance color changes underneath an alliance-colored state. Control requests are allocated once and reused; a `clearAnimationRequest` (EmptyAnimation slot 0) is sent before any solid color.
patterns.whereSeen: C:/Users/ericj/GitHub/9143-2025-A-Updated/src/main/java/frc/robot/subsystems/LEDs.java (195 lines). B has no LEDs at all.
patterns.libraryValue: Highly generalizable and a common team need. PumpkinLib should offer `PrioritizedLeds`: register `(BooleanSupplier condition, Pattern pattern)` pairs in priority order, get the change-detection, the late-alliance re-apply, and the animation-slot clearing for free. The alliance-late-report bug (`displayedAllianceColor` re-apply) is exactly the kind of hard-won detail a library should encode once.

patterns.name: Hand-wired per-subsystem physics simulation
patterns.whatItDoes: Each positional subsystem constructs its sim plant behind `if (RobotBase.isSimulation())` and implements `simulationPeriodic()` with the same 3-step shape: read the sim motor's applied output → drive the WPILib plant with `update(0.02)` → feed the resulting velocity/position back into the simulated encoder. Spark MAX uses `SparkMaxSim.iterate(vel, RobotController.getBatteryVoltage(), 0.02)`; TalonFX uses `getSimState().setRawRotorPosition(rot * gearRatio)` / `setRotorVelocity(...)`.
patterns.whereSeen: A/Elevator.java lines 88-99 + 287-296; A/CorAl.java lines 104-114 + 417-429; B/AlLow.java lines 93-104 + 310-319.
patterns.libraryValue: The `0.02` timestep is hardcoded in all five places, the sim mass/length estimates are private static finals scattered per file, and the TalonFX gear-ratio multiplication is easy to get backwards. PumpkinLib should provide `SimHarness` adapters (`SparkSim.attach(plant, encoderScale)` / `TalonFxSim.attach(plant, sensorToMechanismRatio)`) that own the timestep and the unit conversion, so a subsystem declares a plant and gets sim for free. Also worth encoding: A's Elevator models the cascade as an effective drum radius `Units.inchesToMeters(11.0) / (2.0 * Math.PI)` — a nonobvious trick.

patterns.name: Elastic dashboard tab auto-switching on mode change + one-shot toast notifications
patterns.whatItDoes: `Robot.disabledInit/autonomousInit/teleopInit/testInit` each call `Elastic.selectTab("Setup"/"Autonomous"/"Teleop"/"Testing")`, and `WebServer.start(5800, Filesystem.getDeployDirectory().getPath())` serves `deploy/elastic-layout.json` so every drive-station laptop loads the identical layout via Ctrl+D. `Elastic.sendNotification(...)` fires a toast on a rising-edge failure.
patterns.whereSeen: A/Robot.java lines 62, 93, 108, 126, 142; A/Dashboard.java lines 324-330; vendored util/Elastic.java (390 lines, identical in both repos).
patterns.libraryValue: The `Elastic.java` helper is a vendored third-party file duplicated byte-for-byte — PumpkinLib should just own it (or depend on it) so it's updated in one place.
